sections.title: Unintended Consequences
sections.keyIdea: People respond to an intervention, and what they do next is often the thing that undoes it: a price that is not allowed to ration is rationed some other way.

body.text: The third cause is the one that catches well-designed policies. A market is people, and people respond to a change in the rules by doing something the rules did not anticipate.

The maximum price in Osira flats is the standard case. Excess demand of 100 flats does not evaporate because the price is not allowed to remove it. It is settled by waiting, by who is known to the landlord, by a payment made outside the official rent, or by the property being let for something other than housing. None of those was the intention and all of them follow from it.

A minimum price does the same on the other side. Sellers offer more than is wanted, and if a government has guaranteed the price it now owns a quantity it did not want to buy, with a storage bill nobody costed.

The general form is worth holding on to: **an intervention changes what it is worth doing, and people then do it**. An answer that predicts one of those responses before naming the drawback is doing the analysis the question wants.

realExample.text: Where rents are controlled, landlords quite often find other uses for a property — selling it, letting it to visitors by the night, or leaving it empty. Each of those reduces the stock of rented housing further, which is the opposite of what the control was for.

sections.misconception: Students list unintended consequences as a risk without saying what the response would be. The mark is in the mechanism. Instead: name who responds, what they do, and why the policy gave them a reason to do it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse (6 marks, WEC11) as requiring a chain of reasoning and depth rather than breadth. One consequence traced properly from the incentive that produced it is worth more than four named.

recall.prompt: Sort each response by the policy that produced it.

groups.name: A maximum price
items: waiting lists form for the good
landlords find other uses for the property
payments are made outside the official price
groups.why: Holding a price below the clearing level leaves more buyers than units, and everything here is a way that gap gets settled

groups.name: A guaranteed minimum price
items: more is produced than buyers want
a public agency ends up storing what it bought
growers plant more of the supported crop than before
groups.why: Holding a price above the clearing level leaves more units than buyers, and everything here follows from somebody having to take them

sections.title: Excessive Administrative Costs
sections.keyIdea: Designing, administering, monitoring and enforcing an intervention costs money, and where that exceeds the welfare recovered it is a net loss whatever the quantity does.

body.text: The fourth cause is the simplest and the most often left out of an answer, because it is the one part of an intervention that never appears on the diagram.

In Osira coal the whole prize is $75 a day. That is the ceiling on what any intervention here can be worth. A permit scheme that requires every firm's emissions to be measured, reported and audited could easily cost more than that to run — and if it does, it is a net welfare loss even when it puts the quantity exactly on 50 tonnes.

items: **Designing it** — establishing the number the tool is set from.
**Administering it** — collecting a tax, paying a subsidy, issuing permits.
**Monitoring it** — measuring what is actually happening.
**Enforcing it** — inspecting, prosecuting, and dealing with avoidance.

body.text: Which is why the tools differ so much in practice. A tax uses machinery a government already has. A permit scheme needs measurement built from nothing. Information is almost free. That difference is frequently what decides the choice, and it belongs in any answer comparing them.

realExample.text: Schemes that pay households for a change in behaviour often spend a large share of the budget on checking who qualifies. Where the checking costs more than the payments, the scheme is a net loss however well the payments work.

sections.misconception: Students mention administrative costs as a throwaway line at the end of an evaluation. It is a number that can be compared with the welfare gain, and comparing it is the evaluation. Instead: say what the intervention is worth at most, and what running it would take.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss (14 marks, WEC11) as requiring the validity and significance of arguments to be considered and supported by chains of reasoning. Administrative cost is a significance argument: it can be decisive where the welfare at stake is small.

recall.prompt: Complete the test this cause supplies:
template: The most an intervention here can be worth is the welfare loss it removes: $75 a day
→ against that stands the cost of designing, administering, monitoring and ___ it
→ if the second exceeds the first it is a ___ welfare loss
→ even if the quantity lands exactly on the ___
hints: what has to happen to a rule after it is written, or it is only a suggestion
the word in the specification's own definition of government failure
the quantity the policy was aimed at, which reaching is not by itself enough

sections.title: Moral Hazard
sections.keyIdea: Where an intervention protects somebody from the cost of a risk, they take more of that risk, and the protection then costs more than it was set up to cost.

body.text: The last cause on the list is one you have already met on the market's side in the previous topic: **moral hazard** is being protected from the consequences of a risk and taking more of it as a result.

It appears here because a government protecting people is doing what an insurer does. A guaranteed floor price protects against the price falling, so more of the crop is planted, including on land where it is a poor bet, and the agency buys more than it expected.

What makes this a cause of government failure rather than a cost of the policy is the direction. The protection does not merely cost money; it **increases the thing it was protecting against**, so the bill grows over time and the behaviour it was responding to gets worse rather than better.

The usual answer is to protect partly rather than completely: a floor below the expected price rather than at it, a guarantee with a limit, cover with a share of the loss left where it was. Partial protection keeps some of the consequence attached to the decision, which is the whole point.

realExample.text: Deposit guarantees are the standard case. They are there to stop a panic spreading from one bank to the whole system, and they also mean depositors have no reason to ask whether their bank is lending carefully. Governments respond by regulating the lending instead, which is another tool from this list.

sections.misconception: Students confuse moral hazard with the intervention being expensive. Expense is a cost; moral hazard is the protection making the risk more likely, so the cost keeps rising. Instead: name whose behaviour changes and how the protection changed it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate (20 marks, WEC11) as requiring multi-stage chains of reasoning and informed judgements. Moral hazard is a multi-stage chain by nature: protection, then a change in behaviour, then a cost that was not in the original estimate.

recall.prompt: Match each protection to the behaviour it can change.

pairs.left: A guaranteed floor price for a crop
pairs.right: more of it is planted, on worse land
pairs.why: The floor removes the risk of the price falling, so land that would have been too risky to plant becomes worth planting

pairs.left: A promise that a bank will not be allowed to fail
pairs.right: riskier lending than otherwise
pairs.why: If the consequences of a bad loan are borne by somebody else, the return on a risky loan looks better than it is

pairs.left: Compensation for flood damage to property
pairs.right: building where flooding is likely
pairs.why: A cost that will be met by somebody else does not enter the decision about where to build

pairs.left: Cover that leaves part of the loss with you
pairs.right: care is still worth taking
pairs.why: Leaving part of the consequence attached is what stops the protection changing the behaviour, which is why partial cover is the usual answer

takeaway: Government failure is a NET welfare loss, judged against what would have happened without it.
Five causes and no more, in the specification's own words. A sixth belongs to another topic.
Setting the tax at $30 instead of $15 leaves the same $75 loss, on the other side.

notes.title: Why Governments Intervene
notes.keyIdea: The purpose of government intervention, including reference to market failure.

items.text: Government intervention — action by a government intended to move the quantity traded towards the socially optimal level.
Socially optimal level of output — the quantity at which every cost and every benefit is counted, not only those buyers and sellers feel.
The prize is measurable. Osira coal: market 60 tonnes a day at $60, optimum 50 at $70, welfare loss $75 a day.

The eight methods (1b): indirect taxation (ad valorem and specific); subsidies; maximum and minimum (guaranteed) prices; tradeable pollution permits; extension of property rights; state provision; regulation; provision of information.
Three set a price, one sets a quantity, four set a rule or what is known. A tool that sets one cannot set the other.
An intervention is worth making if it recovers more welfare than it costs to run. That comparison is the evaluation, and the cost of running it never appears on the diagram.

takeaway: Name the failure before naming the policy.
Eight methods and no ninth.
Direction of travel is not the test; net welfare is.

notes.title: Indirect Taxation
notes.keyIdea: Indirect taxation (ad valorem and specific) as a method of intervention.

items.text: Indirect tax — a tax on a transaction, collected from the seller, rather than on income.
Specific tax — a fixed sum per unit; shifts supply in PARALLEL.
Ad valorem tax — a percentage of the price; PIVOTS supply, and the gap widens as the price rises.
Set at the external cost, the curve sellers act on becomes MSC. Osira coal: $15 a tonne takes quantity from 60 to 50.
Two prices after the tax. Pc = $70 off demand; Pp = $55 off the ORIGINAL supply curve. The gap is the tax.
Incidence: buyers $10, sellers $5 — two to one. The RULE is 1.3.4 · 4b, taught in Price Determination.
Revenue = $15 × 50 = $750 a day, using the quantity AFTER the tax.
Evaluation turns on three things: whether the external cost was measured, how much demand responds, and who ends up paying. Where demand barely responds it raises money and changes little.

takeaway: The tax moves SUPPLY. The fall in quantity is a movement along demand.
Specific = parallel. Ad valorem = pivot.
Revenue uses 50, not 60.

notes.title: Subsidies
notes.keyIdea: Subsidies as a method of intervention.

items.text: Subsidy — a payment to the supplier per unit supplied, lowering the curve suppliers act on.
Opportunity cost of a subsidy — the next best use of the money, which is what it has to be judged against.
Osira clinics: external benefit $12 a consultation, market 50 consultations a week at $40, optimum 58 at $44, welfare gain forgone $48 a week.
A $12 subsidy takes quantity to 58. Buyers pay $32; providers receive $44.
The gain splits as the tax burden splits: buyers $8, providers $4 — two to one.
Cost = $12 × 58 = $696 a week, at the quantity AFTER the subsidy.
Only 8 of the 58 consultations are new; the rest of the money lowers the price of consultations that were already happening.

takeaway: The subsidy moves SUPPLY; buyers move down an unchanged demand curve.
Cost uses 58, not 50.
Easy to start, hard to stop: prices settle around it.

notes.title: Maximum and Minimum Prices
notes.keyIdea: Maximum and minimum (guaranteed) prices as a method of intervention.

items.text: Maximum price — a legal ceiling. Binds only if set BELOW the market price. Produces excess demand.
Minimum (guaranteed) price — a legal floor. Binds only if set ABOVE the market price. Produces excess supply.
Osira flats: market $500 a month, 200 flats. A maximum of $400 gives 250 wanted and 150 offered: excess demand 100. 50 who rented before no longer do.
Osira coal: a minimum of $70 gives 50 wanted and 80 offered: excess supply 30.

Minimum price against tax, same market: buyers pay $70 under BOTH. Under the tax the extra $15 a tonne goes to the government ($750 a day); under the floor it goes to SELLERS, and there is excess supply as well.
A price is how a market decides WHO gets the good. Fix it and something else decides: waiting, who is known, or payments outside the official price.

takeaway: Two quantities at the controlled price, not one.
Maximum below, minimum above. A control on the wrong side does nothing.
Same buyer price as a tax; completely different destination for the money.

notes.title: Permits, Property Rights and Regulation
notes.keyIdea: Tradeable pollution permits, extension of property rights, and regulation as methods of intervention.

items.text: Tradeable pollution permits — a fixed total of rights to emit, issued and then bought and sold.
Extension of property rights — giving somebody a claim over a resource that they can defend or sell.
Regulation — a rule, limit, standard or ban, backed by enforcement.
A cap at 50 tonnes makes supply vertical. Buyers bid to $70; the last tonne costs $55 to make; a permit is worth the gap, $15.
That is the tax. A tax names a price and lets quantity settle; a cap names a quantity and lets price settle. Same quantity, same buyer price, different recipient of the $15.
Trading changes WHO cuts, never the total. Cuts go to whoever can make them most cheaply, and nobody has to work out who that is.
A permit IS a property right: a claim that can be defended, bought and sold. That is why permits are tradeable at all.
All three need a fact a tax does not: the right quantity, who owns what, the right limit. All three need monitoring and enforcement, and who is GIVEN the rights decides who keeps the money.

takeaway: Cap and tax reach the same point from opposite directions.
Trading changes who cuts, not how much.
Rights work where a claim can be defined and enforced, and not otherwise.

notes.title: State Provision and Information
notes.keyIdea: State provision and provision of information as methods of intervention.

items.text: State provision — the government supplies the good itself, funded from taxation.
Provision of information — making a fact available or requiring it to be displayed; changes what is known and nothing else.
Under state provision the quantity is set by a BUDGET, not by a price, so free access with a limited budget has to be rationed some other way.
Information moves DEMAND. In Osira clinics, closing the gap takes demand from MPB to MSB and the market reaches 58 consultations at $44.
Same quantity as the $12 subsidy — with buyers paying $44 instead of $32, and $696 a week not spent.
Provision reaches people no priced tool reaches. Information is the cheapest tool on the list and works only if the gap really was knowledge.

takeaway: Provision: budget sets quantity, taxation pays, rationing by something other than price.
Information moves demand, so the price RISES rather than falls.
If people know and still do not act, the campaign changes nothing.

notes.title: Where Governments Intervene
notes.keyIdea: Contexts in which governments may intervene: health, housing, education, transport, environment, energy, agriculture and commodities.

items.text: Context — the setting an exam extract is drawn from. 1c lists eight, and the first job is to say which kind of problem is in front of you.
Health, education — much of the benefit falls on other people, so the market under-supplies. Subsidy, state provision, information.
Housing — there may be no externality at all: the quantity may be right and the price out of reach. Maximum price, state provision.
Transport, environment — costs fall on people outside the transaction, so the market over-supplies. Tax, permits, property rights, regulation.
Energy — the hardest, because both arguments apply at once: external costs argue for taxing it, affordability argues for subsidising it.
Agriculture, commodities — supply is inflexible and demand unresponsive, so prices swing hard. Guaranteed minimum prices, reserves, export restrictions.
Choosing between tools: name the failure, list the tools that act on it, say what each needs the government to know, and judge on which of those facts can actually be established.

takeaway: Eight contexts; say which kind of problem before naming a tool.
Housing and energy are where affordability cuts against the cost argument.
The deciding column is what the government has to KNOW.

notes.title: Government Failure
notes.keyIdea: Government failure as intervention that results in a net welfare loss, and its five causes.

items.text: Government failure — intervention that results in a NET welfare loss, judged against what would have happened without it.

Drawn: a tax of $30 where the external cost is $15 takes Osira coal to 40 tonnes, 10 below the optimum — as far below as the free market was above. Welfare loss $75 a day: the same number as before the government acted.
Information gaps — the tool has to be set from a number nobody can observe, so it is set from an estimate and lands away from the optimum.
Lack of incentives — no rival to lose customers to and no saving to keep, so costs are less tightly controlled than in a market.
Unintended consequences — people respond to the new incentives; excess demand under a maximum price is settled by waiting, by who is known, or by payments outside the official price.

Excessive administrative costs — designing, administering, monitoring and enforcing. The whole prize in Osira coal is $75 a day; a scheme costing more than that is a net loss even at the right quantity.
Moral hazard — protection from a risk increases the risk taken, so the bill grows over time. The answer is partial protection.

Five causes and no more. A cause that is not on this list — however plausible it sounds — belongs to another topic or to another specification, and an answer built on one has spent its words outside what the paper can ask.

takeaway: NET: the comparison is with what would have happened without the intervention.
Five causes, in the specification's own words.
The best case is arithmetic: the same loss, on the other side of the optimum.

quiz.question: The purpose of government intervention in a market is to:
options: reduce the price of the good so that more people can afford it
move the quantity traded towards the socially optimal level
raise revenue that can be spent on other public services
prevent firms in the market from making excessive profits
quiz.explanation: The specification puts the purpose at 1a and ties it to market failure: the market produces too much or too little compared with the socially optimal level, and intervention is an attempt to change the quantity. Revenue and affordability are consequences of particular tools, not the purpose of intervening.

quiz.question: A maximum price will only change what happens in a market if it is set:
options: above the market equilibrium price
exactly at the market equilibrium price
below the market equilibrium price
below the average cost of production
quiz.explanation: A ceiling above the equilibrium is a rule nobody meets: the market was already trading below it. Only a maximum set below the clearing price stops trade happening where it otherwise would, which is what produces excess demand.

quiz.question: Government failure occurs when:
options: a government fails to intervene in a market that is failing
an intervention turns out to be unpopular with voters
the cost of an intervention is larger than the government expected
intervention results in a net welfare loss
quiz.explanation: The specification defines it at 2a as intervention that results in a NET welfare loss. The comparison is with what would have happened without the intervention, which is why an expensive but effective policy is not a failure and a cheap ineffective one may be.

quiz.question: In Osira coal, the market trades 60 tonnes a day and the social optimum is 50. With an external cost of $15 a tonne, the welfare loss is:
options: $750 a day
$900 a day
$75 a day
$15 a day
quiz.explanation: The welfare loss is the triangle: ½ × $15 × 10 = $75. $900 is the total external cost across all 60 tonnes — a rectangle, and a much larger number. $750 is the revenue a $15 tax would raise. $15 is the cost per tonne, which is a height and not an area at all.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the eight methods of intervention the specification lists?
options: extension of property rights
a cut in the rate of income tax
tradeable pollution permits
provision of information
quiz.explanation: The eight at 1b are indirect taxation, subsidies, maximum and minimum prices, tradeable pollution permits, extension of property rights, state provision, regulation and provision of information. A change in income tax is a tax on a person rather than on a transaction in this market, so it is not a method of intervening in it.

quiz.question: A government wants to set a policy that fixes the quantity traded and lets the price settle. It should use:
options: tradeable pollution permits
an indirect tax on each unit sold
a minimum price fixed by law
a subsidy paid per unit
quiz.explanation: Only the permit scheme names a quantity. A tax, a subsidy and a price control all act on the price and leave the quantity to be settled by how the two sides respond, which is why a government that needs a definite total cannot use them.

quiz.question: An intervention that moves the quantity towards the social optimum is still not worth making if:
options: firms in the market object to it and lobby against it
running it costs more than the welfare it recovers
it raises the price that buyers have to pay for the good
it does not reach the socially optimal quantity exactly
quiz.explanation: The test is net: welfare recovered against the cost of designing, administering, monitoring and enforcing the policy. A higher price to buyers is what most of these tools do on purpose, and reaching part of the way to the optimum is still an improvement if it is cheap enough.

quiz.question: A specific tax of $15 a tonne is imposed on Osira coal, where quantity falls to 50. Government revenue is:
options: $750 a day
$900 a day
$3,500 a day
$500 a day
quiz.explanation: Revenue is the tax per tonne times the quantity traded AFTER the tax: $15 × 50 = $750. $900 uses the 60 tonnes traded BEFORE the tax, which is the commonest error here. $3,500 is total spending by buyers. $500 counts only the consumers' share of the tax.

quiz.question: An ad valorem tax differs from a specific tax because it:
options: shifts the supply curve in parallel by the same amount at every quantity
is collected from the buyer at the till rather than from the seller
applies only to goods that generate external costs in production
pivots the supply curve, so the gap widens as the price rises
quiz.explanation: An ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price, so it is a small amount on a cheap unit and a large one on an expensive one — the curve pivots away from its foot. A parallel shift is the specific tax. Both are collected from the seller and both can be used on any good.

quiz.question: After the $15 tax, buyers pay $70 and sellers keep $55. The producer incidence of the tax is:
quiz.explanation: The producer incidence is how far the price sellers keep has FALLEN: $60 − $55 = $5. $10 is the CONSUMER incidence, the rise in what buyers pay, and the two add to the $15 tax. $55 is the price sellers keep, not the change in it.

quiz.question: A tax on a good whose demand barely responds to price will:
options: raise a lot of revenue and change the quantity very little
raise very little revenue and change the quantity a great deal
fall mostly on producers rather than on consumers
have no effect on the price that buyers pay
quiz.explanation: Where buyers have no close alternative they keep buying at the higher price, so the quantity barely moves and the tax is collected on almost the original number of units. That makes it an effective revenue measure and a weak behavioural one, and it also means most of the burden reaches buyers.

quiz.question: A subsidy of $12 a consultation takes Osira clinics from 50 consultations to 58. The cost to the government is:
options: $600 a week
$1,856 a week
$48 a week
$696 a week
quiz.explanation: The cost is the subsidy per consultation times the quantity supplied AFTER it: $12 × 58 = $696. $600 uses the 50 consultations supplied BEFORE it. $1,856 is what buyers spend. $48 is the welfare gain the subsidy was aimed at, which is far smaller than what it costs to capture.

quiz.question: A subsidy raises the quantity traded because it:
options: lowers the curve suppliers act on, so more is worth supplying
raises the demand curve, because buyers can now afford more of the good than before
removes the external benefit that the market had been failing to count in the price
forces suppliers to produce a larger quantity than they otherwise would have chosen
quiz.explanation: The payment goes to the supplier per unit supplied, so it is the supply side that moves; buyers respond by moving DOWN their unchanged demand curve. Nothing compels anybody to produce anything, and the external benefit is still external — the subsidy compensates for it rather than removing it.

quiz.question: Buyers pay $32 after the subsidy and providers receive $44. Compared with the market price of $40, this means:
options: buyers gain $8 and providers $4
buyers gain $4 and providers $8
buyers and providers each gain $6
buyers gain the whole $12 and providers gain nothing
quiz.explanation: The price buyers pay fell from $40 to $32, a gain of $8; what providers receive rose from $40 to $44, a gain of $4. The two add to the $12 subsidy, and they are unequal for the same reason a tax burden is unequal.

quiz.question: A common objection to subsidising a good is that:
options: it lowers the quantity traded below the socially optimal level of output
much of the money pays for units that would have been bought anyway
it raises the price that buyers have to pay for the good at the till
it can only be used on goods that generate external costs in production
quiz.explanation: Only 8 of the 58 consultations supplied are new; the rest of the payment lowers the price of consultations that were already happening. Lowering the quantity and raising the price to buyers are both what a TAX does. And a subsidy is used where a good carries external BENEFITS, not external costs.

quiz.question: A maximum price of $400 is set in Osira flats, where quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. This creates:
options: excess supply of 100 flats
excess demand of 250 flats
no gap at all, because the price has been fixed
excess demand of 100 flats
quiz.explanation: Excess demand is the difference between the two quantities at the controlled price: 250 − 150 = 100. An answer of 250 is the whole quantity demanded rather than the gap; "excess supply" has the direction the wrong way round, since a maximum price leaves buyers unsatisfied; and fixing a price is precisely what stops it closing the gap.

quiz.question: In Osira coal, a minimum price of $70 and a tax of $15 both leave buyers paying $70. The main difference between them is:
options: under the tax the $15 goes to the government, under the floor it goes to sellers
the tax leaves buyers paying more than the minimum price does
the minimum price reduces the quantity bought and the tax does not
the tax produces excess supply and the minimum price does not
quiz.explanation: Both put buyers at $70 and both leave them buying 50 tonnes. What differs is the destination of the extra $15 a tonne — $750 a day of revenue under one and nothing under the other — and that the floor also leaves 30 tonnes offered and unsold.

quiz.question: A minimum price described as a guaranteed price usually also involves:
options: a limit on how much any one producer may sell
a public agency buying whatever is not sold at that price
a subsidy paid to buyers so that they can afford it
a tax on imports of the same good
quiz.explanation: The word guaranteed is a promise as well as a floor: growers may sell at the price, and if nobody else buys at it the agency does. What it buys is the excess supply the floor creates, and storing or disposing of that is a cost of the policy.

quiz.question: When a maximum price stops the price from rationing a good, the good is usually rationed instead by:
options: the government raising the maximum price until the gap closes
suppliers producing more of it to meet the extra demand
waiting, or by who is already known to the seller
buyers agreeing among themselves who should have it
quiz.explanation: The gap does not disappear because the price may not close it, so something else settles who is served: waiting lists, existing relationships, or payments made outside the official price. Suppliers offer LESS at the capped price, not more, which is what created the gap.

quiz.question: Permits are issued for 50 tonnes a day in Osira coal. Buyers bid the price to $70 and the last tonne costs $55 to produce. A permit is therefore worth:
quiz.explanation: A permit is worth the gap between what buyers will pay and what producing costs: $70 − $55 = $15. That is the same number as a tax set at the external cost, which is why a cap at the optimum and a tax at the external cost reach the same place from opposite directions.

quiz.question: Allowing firms to trade pollution permits with one another:
options: raises the total quantity of emissions above the cap
lets firms with more money emit as much as they want
changes which firms cut emissions, but not the total cut
removes the need for the government to set a total at all
quiz.explanation: The total is fixed by how many permits exist, so one firm emitting more requires another to emit less. What trading does is move the cuts to whoever can make them most cheaply, which is what makes the cap cheap to meet — and the government still has to choose the total.

quiz.question: Extending property rights can correct an external cost because:
options: somebody gains a claim they can defend, so the cost enters a decision
the government can then charge a price for using the resource
it converts the good into a public good that nobody can be excluded from
it removes the external cost from the market altogether
quiz.explanation: An external cost exists because the person affected has no say. A defensible claim means whoever causes the harm must buy their agreement or answer for it, so the cost is now inside somebody's calculation. Nothing here makes the good non-excludable — the opposite, in fact.

quiz.question: Compared with a tax, a cap enforced by permits requires the government to know:
options: the right quantity, before any permit is issued
the price elasticity of demand for the good in the short run
the profit margin earned by each firm in the market
nothing at all that an indirect tax does not also require
quiz.explanation: A tax names a price and can be adjusted upwards if the quantity is still too high. A cap names the quantity itself, so it has to be right at the moment it is set — which is why an uncertain optimum argues for the tax and a hard total argues for the cap.

quiz.question: Under state provision, the quantity of the good supplied is determined by:
options: where demand meets supply at the free price
the number of firms willing to enter the market
the external benefit the good generates
the budget the government allocates to it
quiz.explanation: Taking the good out of the market means the price no longer sets the quantity; the budget does. Where free access attracts more demand than the budget supplies, something other than price has to ration it — which is the same problem a maximum price has.

quiz.question: In Osira clinics, closing an information gap moves demand from MPB to MSB. The quantity and price become:
options: 58 consultations at $32
58 consultations at $44
50 consultations at $40
50 consultations at $44
quiz.explanation: Demand shifts right and supply is unchanged, so the market moves UP the supply curve: 58 consultations at $44. 58 at $32 is the SUBSIDY's outcome — the same quantity at a LOWER price, because there the supply curve moved instead. 50 at $40 is the market before anything changed.

quiz.question: Provision of information reaches the social optimum without the government spending on the good itself because:
options: the government requires suppliers to lower the prices they charge buyers
the information reduces the cost of producing each unit of the good
it removes the external benefit from the transaction altogether
buyers who can see the benefit value the good more highly
quiz.explanation: The only thing that changes is what buyers know, and buyers who can see a benefit are willing to pay more for it — which is a shift in demand. Nothing about production costs changes, and no price is set by anybody.

quiz.question: The main limitation of an information campaign as a policy is that:
options: it costs more than a subsidy on the same good
it can only be used where a good has external costs
it changes nothing if the gap was never a lack of knowledge
it lowers the price that buyers have to pay
quiz.explanation: It is the cheapest tool on the list, and it works only on the failure it addresses. If people already know and still do not act, demand does not move and the money is gone — which is why a campaign is usually one of several tools rather than the only one.

quiz.question: The specification lists eight contexts for intervention. Which of these is not among them?
options: banking
commodities
agriculture
energy
quiz.explanation: The eight are health, housing, education, transport, environment, energy, agriculture and commodities. Banking appears in the previous topic as a setting for moral hazard; it is not one of the contexts for intervention that 1c names.

quiz.question: Government intervention in the housing market differs from intervention in health or education because:
options: housing is a public good and the other two are not
the external benefit from housing is much larger
housing markets never reach an equilibrium price
the quantity may be right and the price still out of reach
quiz.explanation: Health and education are under-consumed because much of the benefit falls on other people. In housing there may be no externality at all: the complaint is that the clearing price is unaffordable, which is a distribution problem and needs a different justification.

quiz.question: Energy is a difficult context for a government because:
options: no method of intervention on the specification's list can be applied to it at all
energy markets generate no external costs of any kind in production or use
external costs argue for taxing it and affordability for subsidising it
the government is always the direct supplier of energy in every economy
quiz.explanation: It is the one context where the two arguments in this topic point in opposite directions at once. Many governments tax some fuels and subsidise others in the same year, which is why energy questions reward a judgement rather than a rule.

quiz.question: In agricultural and commodity markets, prices swing sharply mainly because:
options: governments intervene in these markets more often than in any others
the goods are non-rival and non-excludable, which makes them public goods
the external costs of producing them are unusually large and hard to measure
supply cannot be adjusted quickly and demand responds little to price
quiz.explanation: A crop is planted months before it is sold and a mine takes years to open, so supply cannot respond; demand for a staple barely moves with price either. Two steep curves mean a small change in the harvest produces a large change in the price — which is what the guaranteed price is aimed at.

quiz.question: The external cost in Osira coal is $15 a tonne but the tax is set at $30. Quantity falls to 40 tonnes, and the welfare loss is:
options: $0, because the quantity has fallen
$750 a day
$75 a day, the same as before the tax
$600 a day
quiz.explanation: The tax overshoots by as much as the free market undershot, so the triangle is the same size on the other side of the optimum: $75 a day. The intervention has moved the loss rather than removed it, and it costs something to run — which is 2a's net welfare loss exactly.

quiz.question: Government failure has five named causes. Which of these is not one of them?
options: excessive administrative costs of running the scheme
the opportunity cost of the spending
unintended consequences of the policy
lack of incentives to control costs
quiz.explanation: The five at 2b are information gaps, lack of incentives, unintended consequences, excessive administrative costs and moral hazard. Opportunity cost is a real cost of any spending and it is not on that list: a cause of government failure is a route by which the intervention ends up losing more welfare than it saves.

quiz.question: An intervention can be a net welfare loss even when it puts the quantity exactly at the social optimum, because:
options: the social optimum is not in fact the best quantity for society as a whole
designing, administering and enforcing it costs more than it recovers
moving the quantity leaves at least one group in the market worse off than before
the government has no way of establishing what the socially optimal quantity is
quiz.explanation: The prize in Osira coal is $75 a day and that is the ceiling on what any intervention here can be worth. A scheme that costs more than that to run is a net loss however precisely it hits the target, which is why administrative cost is a number to compare rather than a line to mention.

quiz.question: A guaranteed floor price for a crop can cause moral hazard because it:
options: requires the government to store whatever it has bought at the floor
is expensive for the government to administer and to enforce each season
removes the risk of the price falling, so more is planted on poorer land
raises the price that consumers have to pay for food in the shops
quiz.explanation: Moral hazard is protection changing behaviour, so that the thing protected against becomes more likely. The other three are real costs of the policy but none of them is a change in behaviour caused by the protection itself, which is what distinguishes this cause from simple expense.

practice.question: Explain why a government might intervene in a market in which a good is produced with an external cost. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Explaining a reason needs two stages, and the first one is not "because there is an external cost". Decide what the external cost does to the quantity the market settles at, and then what the government is trying to change about that quantity. Keep the chain to one market and take it all the way to the end.
Stage one: the external cost falls on people outside the transaction, so it is not in the private cost the producer pays and therefore not in the price, and the market settles where demand meets marginal private cost rather than marginal social cost (2 marks). Stage two: that quantity is above the socially optimal level, so more is produced than is worth producing and welfare is lost across those units; intervention aims to move the traded quantity down towards the optimum (2 marks). An answer that stops at "to correct market failure" has named the aim without naming the failure or the direction.

practice.question: A specific tax of $15 a tonne is imposed on Osira coal. The price buyers pay rises from $60 to $70 and the quantity traded falls from 60 to 50 tonnes a day. Calculate the consumer incidence of the tax and the revenue the government collects. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
There are two prices in this market once the tax is on, and the first part of the question asks about the movement in only one of them, so decide which before subtracting anything. The second part is a rectangle with two sides, and the question has given you two quantities of which only one belongs in it. Set each stage on its own line.
Consumer incidence: $70 − $60 = $10 a tonne (2 marks), which is the rise in the price buyers pay and not the whole $15. Revenue: $15 × 50 = $750 a day (2 marks), using the quantity traded AFTER the tax rather than the 60 traded before it. Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation involving several stages based on given data and advises showing workings, which is what allows the two stages to be credited separately.

practice.question: Draw a diagram to show the effect of a specific indirect tax of $15 a tonne on a market in which production generates an external cost of $15 a tonne. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Decide first how many curves this needs and what each one is called, because a diagram with the right shape and the wrong labels earns very little. Think about which curve the tax moves and which one it leaves alone, and remember that once a tax is on there are two prices to mark rather than one.
Axes labelled price and quantity, with demand and marginal private cost drawn and the equilibrium at 60 tonnes and $60 (1 mark). A second supply curve above the first by the amount of the tax, correctly labelled as MPC plus the tax — and since the tax equals the external cost it is the same line as MSC, which may be labelled either way (1 mark). The new quantity at 50 tonnes marked on the horizontal axis (1 mark). Both prices marked on the vertical axis: Pc at $70 read off demand and Pp at $55 read off the ORIGINAL supply curve (1 mark). Appendix 6 defines Draw as requiring an accurately labelled diagram using quantitative skills.

practice.question: Draw a diagram to show the effect of a subsidy of $12 a consultation on a market in which consumption generates an external benefit of $12 a consultation. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
This is the mirror of the tax diagram and the commonest error is to move the wrong curve. Work out who receives the payment before you draw anything, because that decides which curve shifts and in which direction. Two prices again, and be clear which of them the buyer pays.
Axes labelled, with demand — marginal private benefit — and supply drawn, and the market equilibrium at 50 consultations and $40 (1 mark). Marginal social benefit drawn above demand by the external benefit, showing the social optimum at 58 (1 mark). A second supply curve BELOW the first by the amount of the subsidy, since the payment goes to the supplier (1 mark). The new quantity at 58, with the price buyers pay at $32 and the price providers receive at $44 both marked (1 mark).

practice.question: Define the term 'subsidy'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate things to say, and the second should not be a rewording of the first. Decide who the payment goes to and what it is paid per, because those are the two features that separate a subsidy from every other transfer a government makes.
A payment made by the government to the supplier of a good (1 mark), per unit supplied, which lowers the price at which any given quantity will be brought to market (1 mark). An answer saying only "money the government gives to help people buy something" has the direction of the payment wrong and does not say it is per unit; both of those matter, because they are why a subsidy shifts supply rather than demand.

practice.question: In Osira flats the market rent is $500 a month. A maximum price of $400 is imposed, at which quantity demanded is 250 flats and quantity supplied is 150. Calculate the excess demand created. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Read the question for which two numbers belong in the subtraction, and in which order. Only one of the figures given is there as context rather than as an input, so decide which before you start. State what your answer is a quantity OF, not just the number.
250 − 150 = 100 (1 mark), which is excess demand of 100 flats a month (1 mark). The market rent of $500 is context and does not enter the calculation. Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation based on given data and advises showing workings, so the subtraction is written out even where the arithmetic is short.

practice.question: Analyse the effects of a guaranteed minimum price on producers and consumers in an agricultural market. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 asks for depth rather than breadth here, so take one chain properly rather than listing four effects. Decide where the floor has to sit relative to the market price for it to do anything at all, and then follow both sides of the market from there — a movement along each curve, in opposite directions.
The floor is set above the level at which the market was clearing, so it binds (1 mark). Consumers move up their demand curve and buy a smaller quantity at the higher price, so consumer expenditure per unit rises while the amount bought falls (2 marks). Producers move up their supply curve and bring a larger quantity forward, so what is offered exceeds what is wanted and excess supply appears (2 marks). Producer income depends on both the higher price and the smaller quantity sold, and on whether a public agency has promised to buy what is left over — which is what turns a floor into a guaranteed price (1 mark). A chain that reaches "producers are better off" without the quantity has stopped halfway; Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a chain of reasoning and depth rather than breadth.

practice.question: Examine whether a government should use an indirect tax or a system of tradeable pollution permits to reduce emissions from an industry. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Both tools can reach the same quantity, so a comparison built on which one reduces emissions will not separate them. Look instead at what each one fixes and what it leaves to be settled, and at what the government has to know before it can set either. Take two points properly and assess them rather than listing five.
A tax names a price and lets the quantity settle, so it can be adjusted upwards if emissions stay too high, and it needs an estimate of the external cost rather than of the right quantity. A cap names the quantity and lets the price settle, so it delivers a definite total, and trading sends the cuts to whichever firms can make them most cheaply without the government having to identify them. Against the cap: the right total has to be known before a single permit is issued, emissions have to be measured firm by firm, and who is given the permits decides who captures their value — auctioned they raise revenue, granted they hand the same amount to existing firms. The assessment should turn on which fact this government can establish and enforce, and on whether a definite total matters more than the ability to adjust. Appendix 6 defines Examine as requiring a chain of reasoning, depth rather than breadth, and a brief assessment of the arguments.

practice.question: Explain how the provision of information by a government can increase the quantity consumed of a good that generates external benefits. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
This tool does not pay for anything and does not set a price, so be careful which curve you move. Work out what changes for the buyer when the information arrives, and let the quantity follow from that rather than asserting it. Two stages again.
Stage one: buyers were unaware of part of the benefit, so their willingness to pay reflected only what they knew, and demand sat below marginal social benefit; publishing the information closes that gap and buyers value the good more highly (2 marks). Stage two: demand shifts to the right and, with supply unchanged, the market moves up the supply curve to a larger quantity at a HIGHER price (2 marks). The rise in price is what distinguishes this from a subsidy, where supply moves and the price to buyers falls; an answer that has the price falling has described the wrong tool.

practice.question: Discuss whether a government facing high fuel prices should subsidise fuel or use the money in some other way. (14 marks)
practice.guidance:
Energy is the context where the two arguments in this topic point in opposite directions, so a one-sided answer will not reach the top. Work out what the subsidy does to the quantity of fuel consumed and whether that is the direction the external costs argue for, then think about who the payment actually reaches and what else the same money could do. Use a specific market and keep returning to it.
For the subsidy: fuel is a necessity whose price falls hardest on poorer households, demand responds little in the short run so a price rise is absorbed rather than avoided, and a subsidy acts immediately where a targeted payment takes time to set up. Against it: fuel carries external costs, so a subsidy moves consumption further from the social optimum rather than towards it and works directly against any environmental objective; the payment goes to everybody who buys fuel, including the households who need it least and who buy the most; the budget cost is large and has an opportunity cost in health, education or transport; and subsidies of this kind are notoriously hard to remove once households and firms have planned around them. Alternatives worth weighing: a payment made directly to low-income households, which reaches the same people without lowering the price of fuel at the margin, and investment in public transport, which changes what the household needs fuel for. A strong answer takes a position, supports it with a chain that reaches a quantity, and says what would have to be true for the opposite judgement to hold.

practice.question: Define the term 'government failure'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
The specification defines this in one line and every word in that line is doing something. Decide what is being compared with what, because a definition that leaves out the comparison has given half the term. Two marks, two separate things to say.
Government intervention in a market (1 mark) that results in a net welfare loss — that is, a loss of welfare judged against what would have happened without the intervention (1 mark). The second mark is the word net: an intervention with drawbacks is not a failure, and an expensive intervention is not a failure. The comparison is the whole of it.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that government intervention to correct market failure inevitably leads to government failure. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
The word to argue with here is "inevitably", and an answer that simply lists interventions that went wrong has not engaged with it. Decide what would have to be true for the claim to hold in every case rather than in some, and find the strongest version of the opposite view before you judge between them. Use one or two markets in depth and keep coming back to them.
For the view: every tool in this topic has to be set from a number the government cannot observe directly — an external cost, an optimal quantity, a benefit per unit — so an information gap is present by construction and the policy is set from an estimate; a tax set at twice the external cost lands the quantity as far below the optimum as the free market was above it, leaving a welfare loss of the same size plus the cost of administering the tax. Add to that the machinery every intervention needs, the responses people make to the new incentives, the weaker pressure on costs where a state provider faces no rival, and the moral hazard that protection itself creates. Against the view: an estimate that is roughly right still recovers most of the welfare, and being approximately right is not failure; some tools need much less to be known than others — a maximum price needs no estimate of an external cost at all, and information provision needs only that the gap be one of knowledge; some tools are administratively cheap because they use machinery that already exists; and the comparison that defines government failure is with the market outcome, which was itself losing welfare. The judgement should distinguish between interventions that are inherently exposed to these causes and those that are not, and should say what determines which of the two a given policy is. A candidate who concludes that failure is common but not inevitable, and who says what makes it more likely, has answered the question that was asked.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of government intervention?
flashcards.back: To move the quantity traded towards the socially optimal level. The reason it is not there already is market failure.

flashcards.front: Name the eight methods of intervention.
flashcards.back: Indirect taxation (ad valorem and specific); subsidies; maximum and minimum (guaranteed) prices; tradeable pollution permits; extension of property rights; state provision; regulation; provision of information.

flashcards.front: Which methods set a price, and which set a quantity?
flashcards.back: Taxes, subsidies and price controls set a price. Only tradeable permits set a quantity. The other four set a rule or change what is known.

flashcards.front: What is an indirect tax?
flashcards.back: A tax on a transaction, collected from the seller, rather than on income. It lifts the curve sellers act on, so the quantity falls.

flashcards.front: Specific or ad valorem?
flashcards.back: Specific is a fixed sum per unit and shifts supply in parallel. Ad valorem is a percentage of the price and pivots supply, so the gap widens as the price rises.

flashcards.front: Where do you read Pc and Pp?
flashcards.back: Pc off the DEMAND curve at the new quantity; Pp off the ORIGINAL supply curve at the new quantity. The gap between them is the tax.

flashcards.front: How is tax revenue calculated?
flashcards.back: Tax per unit × the quantity traded AFTER the tax. In Osira coal: $15 × 50 = $750 a day.

flashcards.front: What is a subsidy?
flashcards.back: A payment to the supplier per unit supplied. It lowers the curve suppliers act on, so the quantity rises and buyers move down an unchanged demand curve.

flashcards.front: How is the cost of a subsidy calculated?
flashcards.back: Subsidy per unit × the quantity supplied AFTER it. In Osira clinics: $12 × 58 = $696 a week.

flashcards.front: When does a maximum price bind?
flashcards.back: Only when set BELOW the market price. It produces excess demand: in Osira flats, 250 wanted against 150 offered, a gap of 100.

flashcards.front: When does a minimum price bind?
flashcards.back: Only when set ABOVE the market price. It produces excess supply: in Osira coal at $70, 50 wanted against 80 offered, a gap of 30.

flashcards.front: What does "guaranteed" add to a minimum price?
flashcards.back: A promise to buy. Producers may sell at the floor, and if nobody else buys at it a public agency does — so the agency owns the excess supply and the cost of storing it.

flashcards.front: A minimum price or a tax, on the same market?
flashcards.back: Buyers pay the same $70 and buy the same 50 tonnes under both. The extra $15 a tonne goes to the GOVERNMENT under the tax and to SELLERS under the floor — and the floor also leaves 30 unsold.

flashcards.front: How does a tradeable permit scheme work?
flashcards.back: A total quantity is decided and that many permits are issued; no firm may produce without one, so supply is vertical at the cap and buyers bid the price up to what the last unit is worth to them.

flashcards.front: What is a permit worth?
flashcards.back: The gap between what buyers pay at the cap and what the last unit costs to produce. In Osira coal: $70 − $55 = $15, which is the same as a tax set at the external cost.

flashcards.front: What does trading permits change?
flashcards.back: WHO cuts, never how much is cut. The total is fixed by the number of permits; trading sends the cuts to whichever firms can make them most cheaply.

flashcards.front: What is extension of property rights?
flashcards.back: Giving somebody a claim over a resource that they can defend or sell, so a cost falling outside a transaction starts falling inside one. A tradeable permit is one.

flashcards.front: What forms does regulation take?
flashcards.back: A limit, a standard, a ban or a requirement, backed by enforcement. It can reach the same quantity as a tax, but every firm has to meet it the same way.

flashcards.front: What is state provision?
flashcards.back: The government supplies the good itself, funded from taxation, so the quantity is set by a budget rather than by a price.

flashcards.front: How does provision of information work?
flashcards.back: It shifts DEMAND rather than supply. In Osira clinics it reaches 58 consultations at $44 — the same quantity as the subsidy, at a higher price and with nothing spent on the good.

flashcards.front: Name the eight contexts at 1c.
flashcards.back: Health, housing, education, transport, environment, energy, agriculture and commodities.

flashcards.front: Why is housing different from health and education?
flashcards.back: There may be no externality at all: the quantity may be right and the price simply out of reach. That is a distribution problem, not a market failure in the 1.3.5 sense.

flashcards.front: Why is energy the hardest context?
flashcards.back: The external cost argument says tax it and the affordability argument says subsidise it. Many governments do both to different fuels in the same year.

flashcards.front: Why do commodity prices swing so far?
flashcards.back: Supply cannot be adjusted quickly and demand for a staple barely responds to price. Two steep curves mean a small change in the harvest produces a large change in the price.

flashcards.front: What is government failure?
flashcards.back: Intervention that results in a NET welfare loss — judged against what would have happened without the intervention, not against perfection.

flashcards.front: Name the five causes of government failure.
flashcards.back: Information gaps; lack of incentives; unintended consequences; excessive administrative costs; moral hazard.

flashcards.front: Give the arithmetic case of government failure.
flashcards.back: An external cost of $15 and a tax set at $30: quantity falls to 40 tonnes, 10 below the optimum, and the welfare loss is $75 a day — the same as before the government acted.

flashcards.front: Why do administrative costs matter so much?
flashcards.back: They cap what any intervention can be worth. The whole prize in Osira coal is $75 a day; a scheme costing more than that to run is a net loss even at exactly the right quantity.

The quantity read off DEMAND and the quantity read off SUPPLY at the controlled price, as two different numbers
The gap between them named: excess demand under a maximum price, excess supply under a minimum price

chains.title: A tax and a permit cap, traced to the same point from opposite directions
steps: Osira coal trades 60 tonnes a day at $60, against a social optimum of 50.
A tax of $15 a tonne lifts the curve sellers act on to MSC, and the quantity falls to 50: buyers pay $70, sellers keep $55, the government collects $750 a day.
A cap of 50 tonnes makes supply vertical, so buyers bid to $70 while the last tonne still costs $55 to make.
The gap of $15 is what a permit sells for — the same number the tax collected, on the same quantity, at the same price to buyers.
chains.result: A tax names a price and lets quantity settle; a cap names a quantity and lets price settle. They meet at the same point, and the $15 a tonne goes to the government under one and to whoever was given the permits under the other.

chains.title: An information gap, traced to a net welfare loss
steps: The external cost in Osira coal is $15 a tonne, but nobody can read that number off a market: it has to be estimated.
The estimate comes out at $30 and the tax is set there, because a policy has to be set from something.
Supply shifts twice as far as it should and the quantity falls to 40 tonnes — 10 below the optimum of 50.
The triangle between demand and MSC over those 10 tonnes is $75 a day: the same loss the free market was producing, on the other side.
chains.result: A net welfare loss, with the cost of administering the tax on top — and nobody in the story was corrupt, lazy or ill-intentioned. One number was wrong, which is why "information gaps" is the first cause the specification lists.

chains.title: Three tools on one market, traced to who ends up with the money
steps: A subsidy of $12 a consultation takes Osira clinics to 58 consultations: buyers pay $32 and the government pays $696 a week.
Closing the information gap instead reaches 58 consultations — the same quantity — with buyers paying $44 and the government paying for a campaign.
State provision reaches people neither of those reaches, because it attaches no price at all, and sets the quantity from a budget instead.
Each tool asks a different question: how much can the budget bear, was the gap really knowledge, and who is excluded by any price at all?
chains.result: The same quantity by three routes, with the cost falling on the taxpayer, on the buyer, or on the taxpayer in a different form. Which is right depends on who the market was failing.

mistakes.title: Calculating revenue or cost with the wrong quantity
mistakes.looks_like: "The tax is $15 a tonne and 60 tonnes are sold, so revenue is $900."
mistakes.why: The tax is only collected on units actually traded, and the tax is what reduced that number. Revenue is $15 × 50 = $750. The same trap works in reverse for a subsidy, where the quantity AFTER is the larger number.
mistakes.instead: Find the new quantity first, write it on its own line, and only then multiply.

mistakes.title: Moving the wrong curve
mistakes.looks_like: "The tax raises the price, so demand falls and the demand curve shifts left."
mistakes.why: A tax is collected from the seller and a subsidy is paid to the supplier, so both move SUPPLY. What happens on the demand side is a movement along an unchanged curve. Provision of information is the one tool in this topic that really does shift demand.
mistakes.instead: Ask who receives or pays the money per unit. If it is the seller, supply moves; if it is what buyers KNOW that changed, demand moves.

mistakes.title: Treating a price control as free
mistakes.why: It makes it cheaper for the people who get a flat and unavailable to some who previously had one. At $400, 250 flats are wanted and only 150 are offered — fewer than the 200 let before the control.
mistakes.instead: Give both numbers: how much cheaper for those served, and how many are not served.

mistakes.title: Saying a minimum price and a tax are the same thing
mistakes.looks_like: "Either way buyers pay $70, so it makes no difference which one the government uses."
mistakes.why: Buyers do pay the same and buy the same quantity. Everything else differs: the tax raises $750 a day that can be spent on the harm, the floor hands the same amount to sellers, and the floor leaves 30 tonnes offered and unsold.
mistakes.instead: Say who receives the extra amount per unit, and whether excess supply appears.

mistakes.title: Thinking permits let rich firms pollute freely
mistakes.looks_like: "Firms that can afford it just buy permits and carry on."
mistakes.why: The total is fixed by how many permits exist, so a firm emitting more requires another to emit less. Trading changes WHO cuts, never how much is cut. The real objections to permits are about setting the total, measuring emissions, and who is given the permits in the first place.
mistakes.instead: Separate the total, which the government sets, from the distribution, which trading decides.

mistakes.title: Calling any disappointing policy government failure
mistakes.looks_like: "The subsidy cost a lot and did not fix everything, so it is government failure."
mistakes.why: Failure means a NET welfare loss against what would have happened without the intervention. A policy that recovers more welfare than it costs is a success even if it is expensive, unpopular or incomplete.
mistakes.instead: Name what the intervention was worth at most — in Osira coal, $75 a day — and set the cost of running it against that.
